messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai is a 31-year-old judge, a role that demands composure, deliberation, and an almost forensic attention to detail. Three years ago, he was driving home from a late session when a flash flood swept his car off a rural road. He remembers it not as a continuous event, but as a series of frozen, vivid snapshots: the wall of brown water appearing through the windshield, the crushing pressure against the driver’s side door, the antiseptic sting of the river mixing with gasoline as he struggled to free his seatbelt, and finally the roar of an ambulance siren as he lay on the embankment, choking on silt. In the months that followed, Kai threw himself back into work, convinced that if he simply didn’t think about the flood, it would fade. He suppressed the images during the day, but at night, a specific trigger could undo all that effort. The first time it happened was during a summer thunderstorm. As the rain began to fall in the same heavy, percussive sheets as that night, the memory would return with full sensory force—he could smell the hospital antiseptic from the emergency room, feel the cold water rising around his chest, and hear the siren’s wail as if it were right outside his chambers. This was not a recollection; it was a complete, terrifying relocation to the moment of the accident. The more the memories assaulted him, the harder he tried to suppress them, but the effort itself left him feeling perpetually on edge.

Kai’s life began to narrow. He started avoiding going out after work, particularly if the sky looked heavy, and he refused to relax at home, believing that letting his guard down was dangerous. He would sit rigidly on his couch, scanning the weather alerts on his phone, his body braced for the next emergency. This constant vigilance, in turn, made him acutely sensitive to any reminder of the trauma. A passing ambulance on the street outside his courthouse would send him into a cold sweat, and the mere whiff of a cleaning solution in the courthouse restroom could trigger the same visceral flashback. The causal loop was tight: a trigger brought the memory, the memory demanded suppression, and the suppression kept him in a state of high alert that made him even more vulnerable to the next trigger. His wife noticed he had stopped laughing, stopped joining her for weekend errands. When she asked why he never wanted to go to the park anymore, he said he just preferred the quiet of the house, unwilling to admit that a cloudy sky felt like a personal threat.

What finally brought Kai to seek help was a moment of professional failure. During a routine sentencing hearing, the defendant’s attorney mentioned a “flood of evidence,” and Kai felt the courtroom dissolve. For several seconds, he was back in the car, the water rising, the siren screaming. He lost the thread of the argument, stammered, and had to call a recess. The shame was immediate and profound. He was terrified that this loss of control could derail his career—that the very composure he had built his identity on was a fragile dam about to break. He came to therapy hoping to learn how to contain the memories, to stop the triggers from ambushing him, but underneath that, he was afraid of what would happen if he ever fully let himself remember.
